 From the Spirit’s semifinal to Division III football: Inside the 2-hour flip of Audi Field
 By Rebecca Tauber Nov. 15, 2026 Updated 9:38 am EST Share article WASHINGTON — Washington Spirit fans, clad in “Rowdy Audi” hats and cherry blossom scarves, erupted with joy Saturday afternoon as their team beat the Utah Royals 2-1.
 But athletes, fans and staff did not have much time to bask in the glory of a third straight NWSL Championship berth. There were locker rooms to clean, soccer fans to usher out and football fans to usher in.
 Two hours later, more than 1,000 cadets marched onto the field led by a pipe band.
 Advertisement
 The Spirit were not technically supposed to play this match at Audi Field, which is owned and operated by D.C. United. With multiple National Women’s Soccer League teams only tenants of facilities, the league was forced to create a contingency plan well before the postseason started.
 With Washington and Gotham FC earning hosting rights in the penultimate round of the playoffs, the former was originally scheduled to host the Royals at Northwest Stadium, home of the NFL’s Commanders, in Landover, Md., to make way for the pre-scheduled Secretaries’ Cup between Division III rivals the U.S. Coast Guard Academy and the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy.
 After a night of logistical scrambling , the groups struck a deal: The Spirit would play at Audi at 12 p.m. ET, avoiding relocation 10 miles away to an unfamiliar stadium, and the Secretaries’ Cup would push kickoff from 1 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. If all went according to plan, that would leave just two hours to transform a professional soccer pitch into a DIII football field.
 On Friday, the field got a fresh spray of paint: soccer lines in yellow, and football lines in white. By Saturday, the takes had come and gone, each fanbase slightly annoyed but happy to be on their promised field, on the promised day. It was time to play some football.
 As part of the compromise, the Spirit played with white football lines on the field. (Scott Taetsch / NWSL via Getty Images) 9:30 a.m. — An hour before gates opened, Angie Kanellopulos stood outside a deserted Audi Field with a box of banners, a stack of D.C. and trans pride flags and a marching drum. Members of the Spirit fan group had taken all their gear with them after the quarterfinal win over the Portland Thorns, unsure where the semifinal would take place.
 “Ultimately, I’m happy it’s at Audi,” Kanellopulos said. “I’m a little frustrated with Audi Field and D.C. United for creating this today, but I’m happy we’re at Audi.”
 Advertisement
 The Spirit have turned Audi Field, a nearly 20,000-seat venue at the edge of the nation’s capital, into a fortress. Saturday’s crowd of 19,365 fans was the team’s sixth consecutive sellout in the postseason, spanning multiple seasons. Despite a string of home losses toward the end of the regular season, the team has leaned heavily on its crowd.
 “You never think it can get louder from the home games that we have and then every game it just gets louder and more passionate,” Spirit forward Trinity Rodman said after the game. “To have so many extra players in a way is really cool.”
 An hour later, the teams warmed up as a local cover band welcomed guests to the fanfare that is Audi Field on game day: face painting, poster making and photos with PK the Eagle. On the field, audio engineers set up microphones and recording equipment in anticipation of the afternoon football game.
 John Malone, D.C. United’s vice president of real estate and infrastructure, sat in his office, projecting calm. The paint was dry; he had replacement sod and 60 extra staff on hand to help clean the stadium and turn over the field. The day was scheduled with a strict run-of-show from the minute gates opened for the NWSL match until football kickoff — as long as the Spirit-Royals game ended on time.
 “Extra time would be a problem,” Malone said.
 The Spirit’s crowd of 19,365 fans marked the team’s sixth consecutive postseason sellout. (Scott Taetsch / NWSL via Getty Images) 12:00 p.m. — The Spirit made sure that wouldn’t be an issue.
 Less than two minutes after kickoff, Utah’s Cloé Lacasse scored the fastest postseason goal in NWSL playoff history, scoring directly off a corner kick. But strikers Sofia Cantore and Clara Luvanga scored two for the Spirit — crucially, in regulation, punching Washington’s ticket to the Championship. Right on time.
 Still, frustration over the scheduling predicament lingered. As with all compromises, each side was left a bit disgruntled — USCGA and USMMA fans with the last-minute timing announcement for a game in the works since last year, and Spirit players and fans with the reminder of the second-class treatment of professional women’s sports. Two weeks earlier, a WNBA Finals game between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries tipped off at 12:30 p.m. ET because of a conflict with a regular-season NBA game between the Atlanta Hawks and Cleveland Cavaliers. And on Sunday, the No. 1 Gotham FC will play their semifinal match against the Kansas City Current in a 5,000-seat, general-admission stadium because of poor conditions at Sports Illustrated Stadium, owned by the New York Red Bulls.

 Inside the NWSL venue saga: Spirit land Audi Field, Gotham move to 5K-seat Icahn Stadium
 The Spirit's relationship with D.C. United helped secure an Audi Field semifinal, while Gotham FC must relocate to Icahn Stadium.
 “Honestly, it’s just insane that in a semifinal game we’re having football lines,” Utah captain Paige Cronin said after the game. “The growth of women’s sports, it’s sold-out arenas. It’s really annoying, but at the same time, we control what we can, and obviously we showed up, we did today, but it is just very disappointing that this is where we’re at in this moment. But I know Spirit, NWSL, I know people are doing everything they can to fix the situation and do the best thing that they could … But end of the day, next year I expect more.”
 Spirit defender Esme Morgan called the lines “a bit disorienting.”
 Advertisement
 “For the most part, didn’t really notice,” she said. “There was only one point where I thought I was on the edge of the area, and then I looked and realized that actually the yellow line was higher, and I was, like, on the edge of the six-yard part.”
 Clara Luvanga and Esme Morgan celebrate a goal on the combination soccer/football field. (Scott Taetsch / NWSL via Getty Images) 2:03 p.m. — As refs blew the final whistle, Spirit players ran to celebrate their historic fifth championship berth while event staff streamed onto the field to remove the goals, install safety padding and assemble the posts. At one point, a group of people passed right in front of Rodman in the middle of an on-camera interview .
 “Guys, move, I’m doing an interview,” she said. “You’re in the way.”
 In one corner, players signed autographs to starstruck kids decked out in Spirit gear. In another, a painting crew began spraying the United Services Automobile Association logo on the grass.
 “We were literally weaving through fans exiting the stadium trying to put signage out,” said Lindsey Bankert, who works for the local printing company responsible for all the Secretaries’ Cup signage.
 Staff had just two hours to turn the field over between the two games. (Rebecca Tauber / The Athletic) 2:43 p.m. — Forty minutes after the final whistle, the yellow lines were the only remaining sign a professional soccer game had taken place. The uprights were upright, the overflowing recycling bins were empty and advertisements for shipyards had replaced the courtside digital banners congratulating the Spirit on the win.
 Because attendance for the Secretaries’ Cup was far lower than the semifinal game — about 8,700 compared to more than 19,000 — Audi Field used only the lower bowl for fan seating, which meant cleaning staff could focus only on that level in time for kickoff. Less than an hour after the Spirit’s victory, future officers of the U.S. Merchant Marines were throwing a football on the field.
 “Pressure makes diamonds,” an event staffer said as he exited the field to make way for the athletes.
 Advertisement
 4:03 p.m. — Approximately 1,000 cadets took the field ahead of kickoff, marching in formation in their coats and caps. Minutes later, cannon blasts announced the Merchant Marine and Coast Guard teams, which ran onto the field led by athletes waving American flags.
 “The Coast Guard’s motto is ‘Semper Paratus’ in Latin; it means ‘always ready,’” said Jordan Gottfried, a member of the Coast Guard at the game, about the schedule change. “One thing that we always like to say is ‘Semper Gumby,’ so we’re ‘always flexible.’”
 U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin did the coin toss. His appearance, along with members of senior Merchant Marine and Coast Guard leadership in attendance, required a higher level of security during the double header.
 “We have all these protectees that are in here, where, if one bomb struck here and took everybody out, we could upset the balance of power in this nation,” said Eric Reed, director of security at D.C. United and former member of the U.S. Secret Service.
 More than 1,000 Merchant Marine and Coast Guard cadets stood in formation on the field two hours after the NWSL match ended. (Rebecca Tauber / The Athletic) 7:48 p.m. — Nearly eight hours after Lacasse’s opening goal, the Merchant Marine hoisted the Secretaries’ Cup, shutting down the Coast Guard 42-14.
 In the coming days, it will all reverse — the breakdown of the goal posts, the removal of the safety padding, the return of the Spirit flags — as the Spirit attempt to become only the second team in league history to win the NWSL Championship at home.
 The pitch, which already had some questionable spots during the semifinal, will require the most attention, starting with the football lines.
 “That’s going to involve a bunch of water, scrub brushes and a lot of elbow grease,” said Ryan Jones, who works with the company doing the painting.
 Next, staff will cut out the parts of the field that featured the United Services Automobile Association logo and replace the sod in those spots.
 Advertisement
 “We’re going to put some grow lights on,” Malone said. “We are going to put some fertilizer on. When you’re painting the grass, you’re painting the tops of it. So as the week goes on, if that grass can continue to grow, I can continue to cut it.”
 Malone is hoping for sunny, warm weather this week to keep the grass happy (the Washington, D.C., forecast shows highs in the mid-60s and clear skies). If not, he has heat lamps and blankets at the ready.
 In six days, the Spirit will return to “Rowdy Audi” for its first home championship appearance. The field will be all theirs by then, alongside either Gotham or Kansas City. There will be no rush to get the fans out, no press conferences relocated to X-ray rooms and no freshly-painted yard lines on the field.
 But some fans’ eyes have grown bigger.
 “Ikea says I can build anything,” a sign in the crowd read during Saturday’s semifinal. “Let’s build a women’s stadium.”
